summary: The server's runtime fidelity is a stack of hard refusals around a few advisory comparisons. Hard (refuse): seal/HMAC on every authenticated read; session-file schema and pre-frontier refusal; stale-write compare-and-swap; the checkpoint gate (activeCheckpoint presence) on next_activity/yield/resume and the five content tools; checkpoint timers (3 s for option_id, ceil(autoAdvanceMs/1000) for auto_advance, none for condition_not_met); option/reply/mode validation; frontier membership for from_activity and delivery activity_id; fan shape refusals; batch bound; contract admissibility; repo/folder containment. Advisory (warn in _meta.validation, call proceeds): activity transition vs graph, version drift, reported exit, step manifest (presence/order/output/declared keys/identity), technique-fetch coverage, activity manifest, variable type/value-set, artifact reconciliation. Record-only: trace events and HMAC trace tokens, activity_outcome, step_completed, progress_published, activity_usage, dispatch/delivery events. Every advisory comparison sets an agent-supplied claim (activity_id, exit, step_manifest, activity_manifest, variables_changed, agent_id) beside a server-held fact (graph, sealed state, history events the server wrote). The server-held facts are themselves partly agent-sourced: history event agentId is whatever agent_id the call passed, step_completed and activity_outcome are written straight from manifests, and an adhoc checkpoint's option list is the worker's own. Docs/fidelity.md describes the seven named layers accurately in substance; it omits several refusals the code performs (frontier resolution, fan refusals, batch bound, STALE_WRITE, schema parse, contract admissibility) and does not note that start_session resume rewrites workflowVersion, that adhoc option lists are worker-supplied, or that trace capture can silently skip when the audit resolver misses.
